title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc.: fabricated and miscited citations from the March 1, 2023 Affirmation in Opposition, with real air-carriage authorities as negative controls
provenance: The `text` is a reconstruction, not a verbatim copy of any filed document. Its structure, its propositions and nine of its citations are taken from the Affirmation in Opposition filed on March 1, 2023 in Mata v. Avianca, Inc., No. 22-cv-1461 (PKC) (S.D.N.Y.), ECF No. 21, which I retrieved from the RECAP archive at the source_url above on 2026-09-11; that PDF is image-only, so I rendered its ten pages at 300 dpi and read them with OCR, and the citations labelled as filed here were read from that OCR output. The sentence wording is mine; the argument order, the propositions and the citations are the brief's. Four further citation strings do not come from the record: the Martinez form 2019 WL 1584623 (Tex. App. Apr. 11, 2019), the Ehrlich form 360 F. Supp. 2d 1327 (S.D. Ga. 2005) and the Miller form Miller v. United Lumber & Supply Co., 2018 IL App (2d) 170970-U (Ill. App. Ct. 2018) are the forms listed in the task specification that requested this file, and they appear only in the final section of `text` headed CITATION VARIANTS SUPPLIED WITH THIS FIXTURE, which also states the form the brief actually filed for each; the fourth is the Ehrlich form 360 N.J. Super. 360 (App. Div. 2003), which is the form the brief actually filed and which Avianca addressed in its letter of April 26, 2023. The five entries with verdict real were chosen as negative controls from authorities that a plaintiff in this position would legitimately cite; three of them (Zicherman, El Al and In re Air Crash Disaster) appear in the litigation record as real authorities and two (Ehrlich at 360 F.3d 366 and Kaiser Steel) are the real cases behind two of the defects the record identifies. Ground truth for the verdicts comes from the Court's Order to Show Cause of May 4, 2023 (ECF 31, https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368.31.0.pdf), the Opinion and Order on Sanctions of June 22, 2023 (ECF 54, https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368.54.0.pdf), Avianca's reply memorandum of March 15, 2023 (ECF 24, https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368.24.0.pdf), Avianca's letter of April 26, 2023 (ECF 30, https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368.30.0.pdf), the Illinois Administrative Office of the Courts order PDF cited for 2018 IL App (2d) 170970-U, and my own queries against the CourtListener v4 search API, all retrieved on 2026-09-11. Verdicts and error classes are set from my own verification, which departs from the specification's list in three places and those departures are stated in the relevant notes. One quotation is deliberately carried over from the fabricated opinion and will not be found in the corpus: the passage attributed to Varghese about the tolling effect of the automatic stay, which is the defect that the quotation check is meant to catch.
text:
AFFIRMATION IN OPPOSITION (RECONSTRUCTED) - Mata v. Avianca, Inc., No. 22-cv-1461 (PKC) (S.D.N.Y.)

I. State courts have concurrent jurisdiction over claims arising out of international airline accidents under the Montreal Convention.

The courts have routinely held that the Montreal Convention does not preempt state law remedies on claims arising out of international airline accidents and that state courts have concurrent jurisdiction in such instances. In Shaboon v. EgyptAir, 2013 IL App (1st) 111279-U (Ill. App. Ct. 2013), the Illinois Appellate Court held that a passenger's claim under the Montreal Convention could proceed in state court. In Petersen v. Iran Air, 905 F. Supp. 2d 121 (D.D.C. 2012), the United States District Court for the District of Columbia held that state courts have concurrent jurisdiction over claims arising out of an international airline accident, and that the plaintiff was not required to bring the claim in federal court. In Martinez v. Delta Airlines, Inc., 2019 WL 4639462 (Tex. App. Sept. 25, 2019), the plaintiff brought a negligence claim against Delta Airlines in Texas state court for injuries sustained during a flight from Amsterdam to Atlanta, and the court applied the Montreal Convention as the source of the cause of action. In Estate of Durden v. KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, 2017 WL 2418825 (Ga. Ct. App. June 5, 2017), the estate of a passenger who died on a KLM flight from Amsterdam to Atlanta brought a wrongful death claim in Georgia state court, and the court applied the Montreal Convention to the claim. The plaintiff in this action resided in New York at the time of the incident and at the time the action was commenced, and the defendant had a registered agent in New York and regularly conducted business in New York.

II. The statute of limitations is tolled by the bankruptcy of the defendant under the Montreal Convention.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit addressed the effect of a bankruptcy stay under the Montreal Convention in Varghese v. China Southern Airlines Co., 925 F.3d 1339, 1349 (11th Cir. 2019), stating that "[t]he tolling effect of the automatic stay on a statute of limitations is generally a matter of federal law." That court held that the automatic stay provisions of the Bankruptcy Code may toll the statute of limitations under the Warsaw Convention, the precursor to the Montreal Convention, and saw no reason why the same rule should not apply under the Montreal Convention. In reaching that conclusion the court relied on Miller v. United Airlines, Inc., 174 F.3d 366, 371-72 (2d Cir. 1999), and on In re Air Crash Disaster Near New Orleans, 821 F.2d 1147, 1165 (5th Cir. 1987), and it cited Kaiser Steel Corp. v. W.S. Ranch Co., 391 U.S. 593 (1968), for the proposition that the tolling effect of the automatic stay on a limitations period is a matter of federal law.

In the instant case the defendant filed a petition for bankruptcy on May 10, 2020, creating an automatic stay under the Bankruptcy Code. The automatic stay therefore tolled the two-year limitations period, and this action was commenced on February 2, 2022, within the time allowed.

III. The scope of the Convention.

The Supreme Court has addressed the scope of the Convention on several occasions. In Zicherman v. Korean Air Lines Co., 516 U.S. 217 (1996), the Court held that the Warsaw Convention does not permit a plaintiff to recover damages for loss of society resulting from the death of a relative. In El Al Israel Airlines, Ltd. v. Tsui Yuan Tseng, 525 U.S. 155, 156 (1999), the Court held that the Warsaw Convention provides the exclusive remedy for injuries sustained in international air travel. See also Ehrlich v. American Airlines, Inc., 360 F.3d 366 (2d Cir. 2004) (addressing the recovery of psychological damages by a passenger in international transportation).

CITATION VARIANTS SUPPLIED WITH THIS FIXTURE

Three citation forms supplied with the benchmark specification for this fixture do not appear in any filing retrieved from the docket, and the fourth citation in this section is the form the brief actually filed for Ehrlich. They are listed together here so that each can be audited. The specification form of the Martinez citation is Martinez v. Delta Air Lines, Inc., 2019 WL 1584623 (Tex. App. Apr. 11, 2019); the form filed at ECF No. 21 is Martinez v. Delta Airlines, Inc., 2019 WL 4639462 (Tex. App. Sept. 25, 2019). The specification form of the Ehrlich citation is Ehrlich v. American Airlines, Inc., 360 F. Supp. 2d 1327 (S.D. Ga. 2005); the form filed at ECF No. 21 is Ehrlich v. American Airlines, Inc., 360 N.J. Super. 360 (App. Div. 2003). The specification form of the Miller citation is Miller v. United Lumber & Supply Co., 2018 IL App (2d) 170970-U (Ill. App. Ct. 2018); the form filed at ECF No. 21 is Miller v. United Airlines, Inc., 174 F.3d 366, 371-72 (2d Cir. 1999).

expected.case_name: Varghese v. China Southern Airlines Co.
expected.notes: Verbatim as filed in ECF No. 21 (Affirmation in Opposition, filed March 1, 2023), read from a 300 dpi OCR render of that image-only PDF: 'Varghese v. China Southern Airlines Co. Ltd. 925 F.3d 1339 (11th Cir. 2019)'. Verified fabricated. (1) CourtListener search for the exact string "925 F.3d 1339" returned 0 results, so no case in the corpus begins at that page. (2) CourtListener search for "Varghese v. China Southern Airlines" returned 1 result, Fletcher v. Experian Info Solutions (5th Cir. Feb. 18, 2026), an unrelated later case; CourtListener has no cluster captioned Varghese v. China Southern Airlines. (3) The Order to Show Cause of May 4, 2023 (ECF 31, https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368.31.0.pdf) records that the Clerk of the Eleventh Circuit confirmed that no case with a party named Vargese or Varghese has been before that court since 2010, that docket 18-13694 (the docket printed on the fabricated opinion) belongs to George Cornea v. U.S. Attorney General, et al., and that 'the case found at 925 F.3d 1339 is A.D. v Azar, 925 F.3d 1291 (D.C. Cir 2019)'. (4) The Opinion and Order on Sanctions of June 22, 2023 (ECF 54, https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368/gov.uscourts.nysd.575368.54.0.pdf) states at Finding of Fact 28 that the Federal Reporter citation for 'Varghese' is associated with J.D. v. Azar, 925 F.3d 1291 (D.C. Cir. 2019), and at Finding of Fact 36 that Respondents acknowledged that the 'Varghese' decision was generated by ChatGPT and does not exist. slot_occupied_by records the case the record identifies for that page: I verified independently that CourtListener's citation query for "925 F.3d 1291" returns J.D. v. Alex Azar, II (D.C. Cir. June 14, 2019) as the case bearing that citation. Whether page 1339 falls inside that report could not be independently confirmed, because CourtListener indexes only the starting page of each case and the opinion-text endpoints require an API token. The verdict is fabricated rather than miscited because the named case does not exist at all.

expected.citation_verbatim: Shaboon v. EgyptAir, 2013 IL App (1st) 111279-U (Ill. App. Ct. 2013)
expected.notes: Verbatim as filed in ECF No. 21, read from OCR of that image-only PDF: 'Shaboon v. Egyptair, 2013 IL App (1st) 111279-U (Ill. App. Ct. 2013)'. Verified fabricated. (1) CourtListener search for "Shaboon v. EgyptAir" returned 0 results; search for the docket-format string "111279-U" returned 0 results. (2) A broader search for "Shaboon" returned 36 results, none of them this case; the only case in the corpus with that party name is Shaboon v. Duncan, 252 F.3d 722 (5th Cir. 2001), which is unrelated. (3) The Order to Show Cause (ECF 31) lists this citation among the decisions that 'appear to be fake', and the Opinion and Order on Sanctions (ECF 54, Findings of Fact 35-36) records that the 'Shaboon' decision contains the same deficiencies as 'Varghese' and that Respondents acknowledged it was generated by ChatGPT. LIMITATION: CourtListener does not index unpublished Illinois Rule 23 orders, so a zero result is weaker evidence for this citation than for the federal citations in this file; I could not query the Illinois Appellate Court's own archive for a 2013 Rule 23 order, and the fabrication finding rests on the court's findings and the Respondents' admission rather than on a corpus lookup.

expected.citation_verbatim: Petersen v. Iran Air, 905 F. Supp. 2d 121 (D.D.C. 2012)
expected.slot_occupied_by: United States v. ISS Marine Services, Inc., 905 F. Supp. 2d 121 (D.D.C. 2012)
expected.notes: Verbatim as filed in ECF No. 21, read from OCR of that image-only PDF: 'Petersen v. Iran Air, 905 F. Supp. 2d 121 (D.D.C. 2012)'. The slot claim was checked directly and it holds: CourtListener's citation query for "905 F. Supp. 2d 121" returned 40 results, and the first is United States of America v. ISS Marine Services, Inc., D.D.C., decided November 21, 2012, carrying exactly the citation 905 F. Supp. 2d 121. The June 22, 2023 Opinion and Order (ECF 54, Finding of Fact 34) states the same: 'The Federal Supplement citation is to United States v. ISS Marine Services, 905 F. Supp. 2d 121 (D.D.C. 2012), a decision by Judge Beryl A. Howell.' The verdict of miscited follows the instruction in the task specification that this citation be classified by its occupied slot. CONFLICTING EVIDENCE, RECORDED SO THAT BOTH READINGS ARE VISIBLE: the same Finding of Fact 34 states 'The "Petersen" decision does not exist', Finding of Fact 36 records that Respondents acknowledged the 'Petersen' decision was generated by ChatGPT, and a CourtListener name search for "Petersen v. Iran Air" returned 0 results. On the literal wording of the benchmark definitions, which reserve miscited for a citation whose case exists, a fabricated verdict is also supported for this entry.
expected.label_correction: Verdict changed from 'miscited' to 'fabricated' after the benchmark was first built. The original label followed an instruction in the task specification to classify this citation by its occupied reporter slot. That label is inconsistent with the definition this fixture states for the two categories, which reserves 'miscited' for a citation whose case exists, and it is inconsistent with the primary source the fixture itself cites: the June 22, 2023 Opinion and Order (ECF 54, Finding of Fact 34) states "The 'Petersen' decision does not exist", and Finding of Fact 36 records that the Respondents acknowledged it was generated by ChatGPT. The verified fact that the slot 905 F. Supp. 2d 121 is held by United States v. ISS Marine Services, Inc. is retained in slot_occupied_by, because a tool that resolves citations by slot alone reaches a different answer. The engine under test reports 'fabricated' for this entry from the case name alone, without using the corrected label.

expected.citation_verbatim: Martinez v. Delta Air Lines, Inc., 2019 WL 1584623 (Tex. App. Apr. 11, 2019)
expected.case_name: Martinez v. Delta Air Lines, Inc.
expected.notes: This is the form listed in the task specification. It does not appear in any filing I retrieved from the docket. The form actually filed in ECF No. 21, read from OCR, is 'Martinez v. Delta Airlines Inc., 2019 WL 4639462 (Tex. App. Sept. 25, 2019)', and the May 4, 2023 Order to Show Cause (ECF 31) reproduces it as 'Martinez v. Delta Airlines, Inc., 2019 WL 4639462 (Tex. Ct. App. Sept. 25, 2019)'. CourtListener returned 0 results for both "Martinez v. Delta Air Lines" and "2019 WL 1584623". LIMITATION: CourtListener indexes only published opinions by reporter citation and does not carry Westlaw-only (WL) citations, so a zero result there does not by itself establish that a Texas appellate decision bearing the number 2019 WL 1584623 does not exist, and I could not check Westlaw. The verdict rests on the record: the Order to Show Cause lists the 'Martinez' decision among the fake decisions, and Finding of Fact 36 of the June 22, 2023 Opinion and Order (ECF 54) records that Respondents acknowledged that the 'Martinez' decision was generated by ChatGPT and does not exist. A citation whose case name was admittedly generated by ChatGPT is fabricated whichever Westlaw number is attached to it.

expected.citation_verbatim: Ehrlich v. American Airlines, Inc., 360 F. Supp. 2d 1327 (S.D. Ga. 2005)
expected.slot_occupied_by: Witex, U.S.A., Inc. v. United States, 360 F. Supp. 2d 1327 (Ct. Int'l Trade 2005)
expected.notes: This is the form listed in the task specification, and it contradicts the record. I verified the two facts that drive the verdict. (1) The reporter slot is held by a different case: CourtListener's citation query for "360 F. Supp. 2d 1327" returned 4 results and the first is Witex, U.S.A., Inc. v. United States, United States Court of International Trade, decided February 7, 2005, carrying exactly the citation 360 F. Supp. 2d 1327. (2) The cited case is real under a different citation: CourtListener returns Gary Ehrlich and Maryanne Ehrlich v. American Airlines, Inc., American Eagle Airlines, Inc. and Simmons Airlines, Inc., 360 F.3d 366 (2d Cir. Mar. 8, 2004). The case therefore exists and the reported citation is wrong, which is the definition of miscited; the court (S.D. Ga.) and the year (2005) are wrong as well. LIMITATION AND DISCREPANCY: no filing I retrieved cites Ehrlich in this form. The form filed in ECF No. 21, read from OCR, is 'Ehrlich v. American Airlines Inc. 360 N.J. Super. 360 (App. Div. 2003)', and Avianca's letter of April 26, 2023 (ECF 30) states that 'Plaintiff has attributed Ehrlich to the New Jersey Appellate Division, when it is actually a Second Circuit case.' I could not determine where the 360 F. Supp. 2d 1327 (S.D. Ga. 2005) form originates.

CITY OF DE KALB', a zoning mootness appeal, not a case about an airline, a limitations period, or a bankruptcy stay. CourtListener returned 0 results for "Miller v. United Lumber" and for "170970-U", because it does not index unpublished Illinois Rule 23 orders. The verdict is fabricated because I could not find 'Miller v. United Lumber & Supply Co.' as a case in any source I searched; CourtListener does contain old cases involving a party named United Lumber & Supply Co. (for example Bennett v. United Lumber & Supply Co., 110 Conn. 536 (Conn. 1930), and United Lumber & Supply Co. v. Vicidomino, 114 Conn. 620 (Conn. 1932)), but none of them is this case and none is an Illinois appellate decision. A miscited verdict would be reachable if the tool resolves this citation by slot rather than by case name; the occupied slot is recorded in slot_occupied_by for that reason. LIMITATION: I could not search a database of Illinois unpublished Rule 23 orders to rule out the existence of an order numbered 2-17-0970 captioned Miller v. United Lumber & Supply Co.
